title: Russia Lifts 2027 Defense Budget 27% to $203B as EU Locks Five Joint Projects Worth up to $190B
subhead: Moscow plans its biggest military budget since 2022 while Brussels approves five European Defence Projects of Common Interest; separately, F-35 stealth components bound for the US are diverted to Hong Kong, exposing a logistics gap in the fighter's global supply chain.

sections.heading: Russia Raises 2027 Military Spending by 27% to $203 Billion
sections.body:
Russia plans to spend 17.1 trillion roubles ($202.6 billion) on defense in 2027, roughly 27% more than the 13.5 trillion roubles ($159.8 billion) originally budgeted, according to government documents seen by Reuters and reported by Defense News. That is the highest figure since the start of the full-scale war in Ukraine in 2022.

The three-year total for defense will reach 50 trillion roubles, or $591.7 billion. The documents also show the government raised its 2026 budget deficit estimate to 3.2% of GDP, up from 1.6%, with total 2026 spending rising 13.2% to 48.6 trillion roubles (20.9% of GDP). To fund it, Moscow plans new tax hikes in 2027, including a windfall tax on metals and mining firms expected to raise about 200 billion roubles ($2.4 billion) annually. Net borrowing rises 26% in 2026 to 5 trillion roubles, and state debt is projected to climb to 21.7% of GDP in 2027 from 19.9% in 2026 — above the 20% level Russian authorities treat as safe.
sections.whyItMatters: The increase is being financed with new taxes and heavier borrowing, not windfall revenue — the budget documents cut projected oil and gas income for 2026 to 7.6 trillion roubles from 8.9 trillion. Russia is choosing to sustain wartime output while its fiscal buffers thin, and the state-debt trajectory crossing the government's own safety threshold signals the cost of that choice.

sections.heading: EU Approves First Five Defense Projects of Common Interest
sections.body:
EU member states approved five joint defense-industrial projects on Monday, making them eligible for funding through the 1.5 billion euro ($1.7 billion) European Defence Industry Program (EDIP), according to the Council of the EU and reported by Defense News. The five areas are: drones and counter-drone systems (DronE/Decoder), air and missile defense (EU-FIAMD), maritime and seabed defense (IMSD), space, and protection of the eastern flank (Eastern Flank Watch).

The European Commission has allocated 325 million euros directly for these projects of common interest, but the indicative investment envelopes are far larger: drones/counter-drone 3.5-5 billion euros by 2033; integrated maritime and seabed defense 43-72 billion euros by 2045; space 24 billion euros by 2034; EU-FIAMD air and missile defense 55-80 billion euros by 2040; and Eastern Flank Watch 60-100 billion euros by 2036. Commissioner for Defence Andrius Kubilius called the approval a 'major breakthrough' with an envisaged funding ambition of around 190 billion euros by 2036. On average 18 EU countries join each project, and Ukraine participates in four of the five.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the EU trying to move from declarations to pooled procurement in five named capability areas. The gap between the 325 million euros actually committed and the 190 billion euro ambition shows how early the mechanism still is — but Ukraine's inclusion in four of five projects ties Kyiv directly into Europe's industrial base rather than treating it as a recipient.

sections.heading: UK Ties Defense to Reindustrialization as Finance Chief Faces a 4.7 Billion Pound Gap
sections.body:
British finance minister John Healey used his first speech to the Labour Party conference to place defense at the center of a 'new age of industrialization,' backing multi-billion pound projects including three new floating docks for submarines at Clyde, Scotland, per Reuters coverage via Defense News. Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said defense spending 'should make Britain stronger in every sense,' pushing a 'buy British' line.

The government faces a 4.7 billion pound ($6.2 billion) gap in its Defence Investment Plan. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to hit NATO's 3.5% of GDP core defense target by 2035, but Healey has not said whether the government will reach 3% of GDP by 2030 — the target he wanted and failed to secure under former premier Keir Starmer, the dispute that led him to resign as defense minister. Healey's first budget is set for Oct. 28.
sections.whyItMatters: Britain is now explicitly selling defense spending as industrial policy to justify it politically. The unresolved question is the 2030 milestone: the funding gap and Healey's silence on the 3% target suggest the near-term trajectory still depends on a budget that has not yet been published.

sections.heading: F-35 Stealth Components Diverted to Hong Kong, Pentagon Investigating
sections.body:
The US Department of Defense is investigating how an Australian F-35A cockpit canopy and weapons-bay door carrying radar-absorbing material were diverted to Hong Kong, where Bloomberg reported Chinese authorities took possession of them, according to Army Recognition. The shipment originated in Australia, bound for the US for inspection, repair or disposal, and stopped in South Korea before being rerouted to Hong Kong. The F-35 Joint Program Office confirmed a 'shipment issue' involving unserviceable components.

Both Australia and Lockheed Martin have played down the risk. Australian Defense Minister Richard Marles said Canberra does not regard the components as technologically sensitive, and Lockheed described the unserviceable items as low exploitation risk. No public evidence shows China arranged the diversion, and the Pentagon has not established that the hardware contained classified technology. As of Sept. 28, no public announcement confirmed the parts' return.
sections.whyItMatters: Radar-absorbing material alone does not hand over the F-35's full stealth design, which depends on shaping, coatings, tolerances and maintenance procedures combined. But a physical part can still reveal materials, construction methods and surface interfaces. The real finding is that the F-35's multinational logistics chain can route sensitive hardware outside its intended security perimeter without detection.

sections.heading: Japan Weighs UK Skyhammer to Build Cheaper Counter-Drone Stocks
sections.body:
British firm Cambridge Aerospace plans to establish production of its Skyhammer low-cost drone interceptor in Japan and offer it to the Japan Self-Defense Forces through a locally supported industrial model, Army Recognition reports. According to Nikkei (Sept. 18), the company has held talks with several Japanese industrial groups and ministry officials, aiming to build a domestic supply chain before formally proposing the system.

Skyhammer is designed to engage Shahed-type one-way attack drones at a fraction of the cost of conventional surface-to-air missiles. Stated specs: a kerosene-fueled turbojet engine, maximum speed 700 km/h, range over 30 km, engagement altitude above 4 km, weight about 17 kg, roughly 2 kg payload, dual-band active radar seeker, and a reload time under one minute. The UK MoD announced in April 2026 it intended to procure Skyhammer for British forces and Gulf partners, with a desert trial in Jordan confirmed on May 1.
sections.whyItMatters: Japan is trying to solve an economics problem — cheap attack drones forcing defenders to spend expensive interceptors. Localizing Skyhammer production both lowers unit cost and reduces reliance on foreign supply chains, extending Tokyo's ammunition-depth strategy beyond its own missile programs.

sections.heading: CENTCOM Says Iran Blockade Has Redirected 122 Commercial Vessels
sections.body:
US Central Command said on Sept. 25 that its forces have redirected 122 commercial vessels enforcing Washington's blockade against Iran, up from 99 on Sept. 11 — a 23-vessel increase in two weeks, per Army Recognition. The USS Boxer, a Wasp-class amphibious assault ship, and the 11th Marine Expeditionary Unit are supporting enforcement, alongside the Arleigh Burke-class destroyer USS Rafael Peralta.

CENTCOM describes the affected ships as 'redirected'; its statements do not establish that all 122 were boarded, seized or detained. The 844-foot, roughly 40,500-ton Boxer carries F-35B fighters, MV-22 Ospreys, rotary-wing aircraft and landing craft, giving commanders an aviation base and boarding-capable Marine force rather than a destroyer-only patrol.
sections.whyItMatters: The cumulative count is the clearest public metric of the blockade's operational tempo. The shift from 99 to 122 in two weeks, with an amphibious ready group as the centerpiece, shows the enforcement mission is scaling rather than winding down — and it is drawing on the same ships and interceptors that are also strained by the Ukraine war.

sections.heading: China Deploys WZ-7 High-Altitude Drone Near Scarborough Shoal
sections.body: China deployed its WZ-7 high-altitude reconnaissance drone for the first time near Scarborough Shoal, participating in exercises around the disputed South China Sea flashpoint, the South China Morning Post reported on Sept. 28. Separately, SCMP reported that Beijing says the US and China will pursue a military crisis-communication pact amid the 2026 Xi-Trump summit track.
sections.whyItMatters: The WZ-7 debut at Scarborough Shoal extends China's persistent surveillance reach over a site it has contested with the Philippines. It comes alongside talk of a US-China crisis-communication channel — a signal that both sides are willing to pair harder operational signaling with mechanisms to manage escalation.

bottomLine: Two fiscal decisions dominated the day: Russia's 2027 defense budget rising 27% to $202.6 billion and the EU clearing five joint defense projects with an eventual 190 billion euro ambition. Both point to a war economy and a peacetime bloc each trying to lock in multi-year industrial output, though the EU's committed cash (325 million euros) remains a small fraction of its stated goals. Elsewhere, the F-35 Hong Kong diversion exposed a real, if likely limited, supply-chain security gap, Japan moved to localize cheap counter-drone interceptors, and CENTCOM's vessel-redirection count climbed to 122 — evidence the Iran blockade is expanding even as the same interceptor stocks strain under demand from Ukraine.
sources: Defense News (Reuters), Defense News, Council of the EU, European Commission, Army Recognition, Nikkei, South China Morning Post, Bloomberg, US CENTCOM
